Postgraduate certificates and diplomas, which are structured programmes over months or years that give a vet deeper expertise in an area like surgery, internal medicine or dermatology. Shorter continuing professional development courses, usually called CPD, such as webinars and short courses. And training for whole practice teams.

**NORA:** In what format?

**JAMES:** Online, blended, meaning a mix of online study and in-person sessions, and fully in person. ### How vets keep learning

**NORA:** For people outside the profession, why do vets need training after they qualify?

**JAMES:** In general, for the same reasons doctors do. Veterinary medicine changes. New drugs, new diagnostic tools, new surgical techniques, new evidence. And in the UK, the professional regulator, the Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons, sets requirements for continuing professional development, so vets and veterinary nurses are expected to keep learning and record it each year. I won't quote the exact hours, but it's a real, ongoing requirement.

**NORA:** So there's a baseline of demand built in.

**JAMES:** Exactly. That's one of the attractions of this market. CPD is close to mandatory, so it's bought steadily, year in, year out. It's not a discretionary purchase in the way a lot of training is.

**NORA:** And postgraduate certificates are different?

**JAMES:** Yes. They're a bigger commitment. A vet who wants to become the go-to person for orthopaedic surgery in their practice, or wants to move into a referral role, might take a postgraduate certificate over a year or more. That involves study modules, assignments, case reports and assessments. It's more like a part-time degree. It costs more and it's a career decision.

**NORA:** Referral role. Explain the career ladder.

**JAMES:** In general terms, most vets start in first-opinion practice, the local clinic where pet owners bring their animals. Over time, some develop a special interest and take further qualifications. At the top are specialists, who have completed long, demanding training and often work in referral hospitals, where first-opinion vets send complex cases. In between, there's a large group of experienced vets with advanced skills in a particular area, and in the UK the regulator recognises a level of advanced practitioner status for vets with relevant postgraduate qualifications. I won't go into the exact criteria.

**NORA:** So postgraduate certificates sit in that middle band.

**JAMES:** That's the sweet spot, in my view. It's a big population of vets who want to progress without committing to full specialist training. They want something recognised, practical and compatible with a full-time job. A provider that serves that band well has a durable market, because each year a new cohort of vets reaches that stage of their career.

**NORA:** And it's good for the practice too.

**JAMES:** Very. A first-opinion practice with a vet who has advanced skills in, say, ultrasound or dentistry can keep more cases in-house instead of referring them. That's better for the practice's revenue and often more convenient for the pet owner. So employers have a clear financial reason to fund this training.

**NORA:** Who pays? The vet or the practice?

**JAMES:** Both, in general. Many practices give vets a CPD budget and time off for training. For bigger programmes, the practice may pay in return for the vet staying for a period. Independent vets or those moving between jobs may pay themselves. And increasingly, large practice groups buy training centrally.

**NORA:** Tell me about those groups.

**JAMES:** This is one of the biggest changes in the profession. Over the past decade or so, a large share of UK vet practices have been bought by corporate groups, many backed by private equity or large companies. Instead of thousands of independent practices each buying training separately, you have groups with hundreds of practices that negotiate training centrally. The UK's competition regulator has been looking closely at the vet market in recent years, which tells you how significant that consolidation has become.

**NORA:** And that changes how training is sold.

**JAMES:** Completely. Selling to a group means negotiating a contract for many vets and nurses, often with subscriptions or bulk access. The group wants consistent quality, good reporting on who's done what, and a fair price per head. A training provider that can't offer that kind of account management struggles to win group business.

**NORA:** You also mentioned a vet shortage.

**JAMES:** Yes. The UK has had well-publicised difficulties recruiting and keeping enough vets and nurses in recent years, in general. That cuts both ways for a training company. Fewer vets means fewer learners. But practices that are short-staffed need their existing people to be more capable, and they use training and career development to keep staff. A clear path to a postgraduate certificate can be a reason to stay with an employer.

**NORA:** And online has taken over?

**JAMES:** A lot of it. A survey reported in the veterinary trade press said online webinars now make up about three quarters of annual CPD for the members of one webinar provider. That's a specific group of people who already like webinars, so it's not representative of all vets. But the direction is clear. Short CPD has moved heavily online.

**NORA:** And veterinary nurses?

**JAMES:** They're a big and sometimes overlooked audience. Nurses also have CPD requirements, and their role has been expanding. Training for the whole practice team, from nurses to receptionists to practice managers, is part of this market too.

### Inside the offer

**NORA:** What does an Improve course look like, from the learner's side?

**JAMES:** We have limited detail, so let me describe the general shape of postgraduate veterinary programmes and what we know of Improve's formats. A learner registers, gets access to an online learning platform. We've seen the name MyImprove associated with that. They work through modules, which may be video lectures, reading, quizzes and case discussions. For blended programmes, they attend practical sessions in person. And they submit assignments and case reports that are marked by tutors, usually experienced specialists.

**NORA:** So there's a lot of human expertise in it.

**JAMES:** A great deal. The course content is written by specialists. The marking and feedback are done by specialists. The practical sessions are taught by specialists. That's the quality of the product, and it's also the cost.

**NORA:** And the practical sessions. Why can't those go online?

**JAMES:** Some skills simply need hands. Surgical technique, handling instruments, using imaging equipment, examining an animal. In general, veterinary practical training uses models, simulators and sometimes cadaver material, under close supervision. That's expensive to run, because you need a venue, equipment and specialists in the room, but it's also hard to copy, which protects that part of the business from cheap online competition.

**NORA:** So the physical training centre is a moat, of sorts.

**JAMES:** A modest one, yes. Improve's news pages talk about a world-leading veterinary training centre, though we couldn't read the details. If it has invested in high-quality practical facilities, that's an asset general AI can't touch.

**NORA:** Are these certificates accredited by someone?

**JAMES:** In general, postgraduate veterinary certificates in the UK are often validated or accredited in partnership with a university or a recognised awarding body, which is what gives them weight on a CV. We didn't confirm Improve's current accreditation arrangements, so I won't name any. But recognition is a key part of what learners are buying, and it's another thing that separates a postgraduate programme from a webinar.

**NORA:** And the short CPD?

**JAMES:** More scalable. A recorded webinar or an online module can be sold to many vets with little extra cost per learner. That's the part of the market where price competition is strongest, because there are lots of providers.

**NORA:** And the languages?

**JAMES:** If the multi-language description is right, Improve offers courses in several languages, which suggests an international business beyond the UK. Veterinary postgraduate training is in demand in many countries, and a provider with an established curriculum can take it abroad, either in English or translated. But translation and adaptation are expensive and slow if done entirely by hand.

**NORA:** Do we know what share of the business is international?

**JAMES:** We don't. That's one of the big unknowns. It could be a small add-on or a large part of revenue. The fact that the company calls itself International, and that the description mentions several languages, suggests it's meaningful, but we can't size it.

**NORA:** And the "Online Bitesize CPD" thing?

**JAMES:** At the London Vet Show, Improve offered an online bitesize CPD package as a prize. That's a small detail, but it hints at subscription or bulk access products, which fit the trend towards selling to practices and groups rather than one course at a time.

### The market and competitors

**NORA:** How big is the market?

**JAMES:** We couldn't find a reliable figure. Several market research vendors publish reports on veterinary education and veterinary continuing education platforms, but the snippets we could see contained no figures we'd trust. So we won't quote a number.

**NORA:** What drives demand, in your view?

**JAMES:** Four things. Regulatory CPD requirements, which create a steady baseline. Consolidation of practices into groups, which centralises buying and creates larger contracts. Staff shortages, which push employers to develop and retain their people. And international demand for English-language postgraduate training from established providers.

**NORA:** Who are the competitors?

**JAMES:** The Webinar Vet, based in Liverpool, is a well-known online veterinary CPD provider that started as a founder-led business. We didn't verify its current ownership. Legacy Education and Encore Vet appear as comparable vet education providers in industry comparison listings. Veterinary Growth Partners also appears as a comparable, but we didn't open its profile. In North America, the North American Veterinary Community, known as NAVC, runs large CPD conferences and online learning. And universities, such as Scotland's Rural College, provide veterinary and animal science education.

**NORA:** And Suveto?

**JAMES:** Suveto, with Veterinary Study Groups, appears in comparison lists as a competitor too. But since it's also owned by Levine Leichtman, it's better thought of as a sister company. They may overlap in some areas. They may also complement each other.

**NORA:** How do providers differentiate?

**JAMES:** In general, by the quality and reputation of their tutors, the recognition of their qualifications, the convenience of the format, and price. For postgraduate certificates, reputation and recognition dominate. A vet is investing a year of their life. For short CPD, convenience and price dominate.

**NORA:** Tell me a bit more about the webinar model, since that's where the price pressure is.

**JAMES:** In general, webinar providers record or broadcast live talks from experts, and sell access either one at a time or through memberships. Once a talk is recorded, it can be sold to thousands of vets at almost no extra cost. That makes membership pricing very competitive. The model suits busy vets who want to fit learning into a lunch break or an evening.

**NORA:** And the big conferences?

**JAMES:** Organisations like NAVC in North America run very large events where thousands of vets gather for lectures and exhibitions, and many have built online learning around them. They have scale and brand, and they compete for the same CPD hours. For a company like Improve, they're both competition and, potentially, partners or channels in other markets.

**NORA:** And AI-native competitors?

**JAMES:** None found specifically in veterinary education. But the general AI threat is real. Any vet can ask a general AI assistant about a clinical topic. That won't give them a recognised qualification or practical skills, but it may reduce what they're willing to pay for basic CPD content.

**NORA:** Should we worry about AI giving vets clinical answers?

**JAMES:** That's a profession-wide issue, not a company one. In general, vets, like doctors, are cautious about relying on general AI for clinical decisions, and rightly so. But it does change expectations. Vets will increasingly expect learning to be available instantly, at the point of need, in a conversational form. Training providers that offer trusted, evidence-based answers in that format may win.

### Into human healthcare

**NORA:** Let's talk about Finium. Why would a veterinary education company buy a human healthcare education company?

**JAMES:** We only know what the announcements' titles say: that Improve acquired Finium, an Italian human healthcare education company, to expand into human healthcare education. So any reasoning is ours.

**NORA:** Go on, then.

**JAMES:** The capabilities overlap. Postgraduate and continuing education for healthcare professionals, whether they treat animals or people, involves the same kinds of work: specialist-written content, structured programmes, practical sessions, assessment, accreditation and a learning platform. A company that is good at running that machine for vets could, in theory, run it for doctors, dentists, nurses or other professionals.

**NORA:** And the human market is much bigger.

**JAMES:** In general, yes, far bigger than the veterinary one. Continuing education for medical professionals is a large international market. So Finium gives Improve a foothold in a much larger space, and in Italy, a new country.

**NORA:** What's the risk?

**JAMES:** Focus. Human healthcare education has its own regulators, accreditation systems, competitors and relationships. Each country has its own rules for medical continuing education. It's not as simple as relabelling a veterinary course. And integrating a company in another country, with another language, takes management time.

**NORA:** Is Italy a particular kind of market for this?

**JAMES:** In general terms, Italy has a formal national system of continuing education for healthcare professionals, known by its Italian initials, E C M, under which professionals are expected to earn credits over a period through accredited courses. I won't describe the details, and we didn't find what Finium specifically offers. But a market with a formal credit system tends to create steady, recurring demand, much like CPD requirements do for UK vets. That may be part of the appeal.

**NORA:** So it's the same shape of demand, just with people instead of animals.

**JAMES:** That's our reading. Mandatory learning, structured credits, and professionals who are busy and want convenient formats. If Improve's production and delivery model works in one, it plausibly works in the other.

**NORA:** How would you make it pay off?

**JAMES:** In my view, by sharing the production machine rather than the content. The tools, processes and platforms for making, translating, delivering and marking courses could serve both sides. If Improve builds an AI-assisted production and localisation process, it can use it for both veterinary and human healthcare courses. That's where the real synergy would be.

### A vet's postgraduate year, step by step

**NORA:** Let's make it concrete. Walk me through a learner's year. Invented, not a real person.

**JAMES:** Meet Priya, a small-animal vet, four years out of vet school, working at a practice that's part of a mid-sized group in the Midlands. She's interested in surgery and wants to become the practice's lead for soft tissue procedures. Her clinical director suggests a postgraduate certificate, and the group agrees to pay, as long as she commits to staying.

**NORA:** What does her year look like?

**JAMES:** She enrols in September. Each month, there's a module online: recorded lectures, reading, and a quiz. She studies in the evenings, after long shifts. Every few months, she travels to a practical session where she works on surgical skills with a tutor. And she has to write case reports, detailed write-ups of real cases she's managed, which are marked by a specialist.

**NORA:** What's hard about it?

**JAMES:** Time, mostly. Priya works full time in a busy practice that's short of staff. She often falls behind on modules. When she submits a case report, she waits several weeks for feedback, because the tutors are practising specialists who mark in their spare time. By the time she gets feedback, she's already started the next report, and she's repeated the same mistake.

**NORA:** That sounds frustrating.

**JAMES:** It's a common complaint in many part-time postgraduate programmes, in general. Slow feedback, isolation, and difficulty fitting study around work. Some learners drop out.

**NORA:** Now replay it with AI in the picture.

**JAMES:** Okay. Priya still studies the same modules, written by specialists. But now, when she drafts a case report, she can get instant formative feedback from an AI assistant trained on the programme's marking criteria. It tells her that her discussion of the differential diagnoses is thin, that she hasn't referenced recent evidence, and that her structure doesn't match what the assessors expect. She revises before submitting.

**NORA:** So the specialist tutor still marks it.

**JAMES:** Absolutely. The final mark and the expert feedback come from a human specialist. But because Priya's draft is stronger, the tutor spends less time on basics and more on the clinical reasoning that only a specialist can judge. And the tutor might have an AI tool that drafts first-pass comments against the criteria, which the tutor edits, so feedback comes back in days rather than weeks.

**NORA:** And between modules?

**JAMES:** Priya can ask a course assistant questions about the material at eleven at night, after a shift, and get answers grounded in the course content, with references. She can also get short refreshers on topics she's struggling with. And if she's falling behind, the platform nudges her, and perhaps her tutor, before she drops out.

**NORA:** And her employer?

**JAMES:** The group's learning lead gets a simple report: Priya is on track, she's completed these modules, her case reports are improving. That's important for the group, which is paying and wants to know it's working.

**NORA:** So again, AI isn't replacing the expert. It's making the expert's time count.

**JAMES:** That's the theme. In professional education, the scarce resource is specialist time. AI should be used to protect it and focus it, not to pretend it's unnecessary.

**NORA:** Let's look at the same story from the employer's side. The group that's paying.

**JAMES:** Sure, still invented. Meet Helen, head of clinical development at the group Priya works for, with around a hundred and fifty practices. Every year she has a training budget, a board asking what it buys, and a recruitment team telling her that career development is one of the main reasons vets join or leave. Today, she buys training from several providers, each with its own reports, spreadsheets and invoices.

**NORA:** So she can't see the whole picture.

**JAMES:** Not easily. She knows roughly how many vets are on postgraduate programmes, but not who's falling behind, which practices are short of CPD hours, or whether the vets who completed certificates stayed longer. When the budget review comes, she argues from anecdotes.

**NORA:** And in the better version?

**JAMES:** She has one dashboard from her main provider showing every learner's progress, CPD hours by practice, completion rates, and, linked with the group's own HR data under proper safeguards, whether trained vets stay longer. An AI assistant can answer questions like, which practices have no one working towards a dentistry qualification, or which learners are at risk of not completing this term. She can intervene early and make the case for her budget with evidence.

**NORA:** And the provider who gives her that wins the contract renewal.

**JAMES:** In my view, very likely. In a consolidated market, the provider that makes the group's learning lead look good is the one that keeps the account.

### Digital and AI today

**NORA:** Where is Improve with AI today?

**JAMES:** We found nothing public. No AI product features, no AI partnerships and no AI hires. A description of the business we saw notes no AI messaging. The company does have a digital learning platform, and it runs online courses, so the digital foundation is there.

**NORA:** Is that a surprise?

**JAMES:** Not really. Professional education providers, especially in clinical fields, tend to be cautious. Accuracy and reputation matter enormously. And many are focused on running their programmes rather than on technology. But the absence of anything public does mean there's an opportunity to move.

**NORA:** What about course production? Is that manual?

**JAMES:** One description we saw suggests course production is manual, but we couldn't verify it. In general, for many providers, making a course involves specialists writing content, instructional designers shaping it, media teams producing video, and translators adapting it for other languages. That's a lot of human effort per course.

**NORA:** Is there useful data sitting in the platform already?

**JAMES:** Probably, though we can't see it. Any online learning platform collects information on which modules people start and finish, where they drop off, how they score on quizzes and how long assignments take to mark. For a provider thinking about AI, that's the starting point. It tells you which courses are worth translating first, where learners struggle and need more support, and where tutor time is going. Before buying any AI tool, I'd want a clear look at that data.

**NORA:** And competitors?

**JAMES:** We didn't find AI announcements from the vet education competitors either. So, as in some of our other episodes, the category seems early. Whoever builds a credible AI-assisted model first, with quality intact, could gain an advantage.

**NORA:** What does AI in professional education usually look like, in general?

**JAMES:** A few common patterns across the industry. Course assistants that answer learners' questions from the course material. Tools that help instructional designers turn specialist notes into structured modules and quizzes. Automatic captions and translation. Analytics that flag learners who are falling behind. And, more experimentally, simulated cases where the learner works through a virtual patient. None of these are exotic any more. The question is whether a provider applies them carefully, with experts checking the outputs.

### The challenges

**NORA:** Let's talk challenges.

**JAMES:** First, exposure to UK vet practice spending. If practices are under financial pressure, or if staff shortages mean they can't release people for training, demand can suffer. That's our inference, but it's a real sensitivity.

**NORA:** Second?

**JAMES:** Concentration of buyers. As practice groups consolidate, a smaller number of large buyers control a larger share of training budgets. That gives them negotiating power, and losing one big group contract would hurt.

**NORA:** Third?

**JAMES:** Price pressure in basic CPD from low-cost webinar providers and, increasingly, from free content and general AI. The postgraduate end is more protected, but the short CPD end is crowded.

**NORA:** Fourth?

**JAMES:** The cost of specialist time. Content writing, marking and practical teaching all rely on experienced specialists who are in short supply and have day jobs. That limits how fast the business can grow and keeps costs high.

**NORA:** Fifth?

**JAMES:** Integration and focus. Several ownership changes, a move into human healthcare through Finium, and possibly a relationship with Suveto to work out. Each takes management attention. And with very little public information, it's hard to judge how well these are going.

**NORA:** And visibility generally?

**JAMES:** It's a real issue for anyone outside trying to assess the company, including potential partners and, eventually, buyers. No public leadership information that we could read, few dated news items, no financial figures. That's not unusual for a private company, but it's an extreme case.

**NORA:** And AI itself as a challenge for the assessments?

**JAMES:** Yes, that's a near-term one for every education provider, in general. If a learner can ask a general AI tool to draft a case report or an essay, written assignments become less reliable as evidence of skill. Providers need to adapt, with more emphasis on real case data, practical assessments, oral examinations and reflective work that's hard to fake. That's extra cost and design work, and it lands on the same scarce specialists.

### Opportunities

**NORA:** Okay, opportunities. You're on the board.

**JAMES:** First, AI-assisted course localisation. Take existing courses and use AI to translate and adapt them into other languages, with specialists reviewing the clinical content and native speakers checking the language. That could cut the time and cost of launching a new language edition dramatically.

**NORA:** Why is that the top one?

**JAMES:** Because, if the multi-language description is right, Improve already sells in several languages, so the demand is proven. The cost is the bottleneck. AI translation and subtitling have become very capable, and they're well suited to structured educational content. The saving is direct and measurable, and faster launches mean more revenue.

**NORA:** Second?

**JAMES:** AI-assisted marking and feedback, as in Priya's story. Formative feedback for learners before submission, and draft comments for tutors. That reduces tutor hours per assignment and speeds up feedback, which should improve completion rates and satisfaction.

**NORA:** Third?

**JAMES:** Pricing and bundling for practice groups. Subscriptions with seat-based pricing, clear reporting for the group's learning lead, and bundles combining CPD and postgraduate pathways. Usage data can help price fairly and show value.

**NORA:** Fourth?

**JAMES:** Working with Suveto. If Suveto's study groups and Improve's courses serve the same vets, there could be a natural path: a vet who attends study groups moves on to a postgraduate certificate, or vice versa. We found no evidence of any current link, so this is purely an idea. And any cooperation between two companies owned by the same firm has to make sense for each one's customers.

**NORA:** Fifth?

**JAMES:** Finium integration, by sharing production tools between veterinary and human healthcare education, as we discussed. Then international expansion, focusing on markets with demand for English-language or translated postgraduate training and with CPD requirements. And possibly acquisitions of smaller CPD providers to consolidate the UK market.

**NORA:** And veterinary nurses specifically?

**JAMES:** I'd single them out as an opportunity, in general. The nursing role in UK practices has been growing, and there's a lot of discussion in the profession about letting nurses do more, which would need more training. Nurses are numerous, have their own CPD needs, and are often under-served compared with vets. Shorter, practical, affordable programmes for nurses, with AI-supported study, could be a growth segment. We don't know how large Improve's nursing offer is today.

**NORA:** And back to Suveto for a moment. What would a sensible first step look like?

**JAMES:** Something small and low-risk, in my view. Share learner research, so both companies understand what vets want at different career stages. Perhaps cross-refer learners where one company has a course and the other doesn't. And if both are building AI tools, compare notes on vendors and governance rather than building the same thing twice. Anything bigger would be a decision for the owner, and we have no evidence it's being considered.

**NORA:** What about AI products for vets in practice?

**JAMES:** It's an intriguing idea. A trusted, evidence-based assistant for vets, built on Improve's course content, that answers clinical learning questions with references. That moves Improve from selling courses to supporting vets day to day. But it carries real responsibility. Clinical questions in practice are high stakes, and the line between learning support and clinical decision support has to be very clear. I'd treat it as a later bet, after the internal uses are proven.

**NORA:** You mentioned virtual patients. Is that realistic for vets?

**JAMES:** As a learning tool, I think it's one of the most exciting ideas. Imagine a simulated case: a cat with weight loss and increased thirst. The learner asks the virtual owner questions, chooses tests, sees results, and decides on treatment. The AI plays the owner and reveals information based on what the learner asks. At the end, a structured debrief compares the learner's reasoning with an expert's approach.

**NORA:** Like the negotiation role-play from our Skill Dynamics episode.

**JAMES:** Very similar idea. Practice in a safe setting. And it suits clinical reasoning well, because the skill is asking the right questions in the right order. The cases would have to be designed and checked by specialists, so the AI doesn't invent unrealistic findings. But a library of virtual cases could be a premium product, and it's hard for a general chatbot to replicate well.

**NORA:** And for the practice groups?

**JAMES:** Analytics. A group's learning lead wants to see, across hundreds of vets and nurses, who has done what, where skills gaps are, and whether training is linked to retention. If Improve can provide that reporting well, it becomes much harder for a group to switch to a cheaper provider.

### The best AI bet and the first 100 days

**NORA:** One bet?

**JAMES:** AI-assisted course localisation and production across the language catalogue. It uses an asset the business already has, its courses. It addresses a cost that's likely large and manual. And the result, more courses in more languages, faster, is easy to measure.

**NORA:** How would you run it?

**JAMES:** Days one to thirty: pick one successful course that already exists in English and one target language where there's demand. Measure the baseline: how long and how much the last translation took, from start to launch, and who was involved. Choose the tools, for translation, subtitles and voice, and set the quality bar with clinical specialists.

**NORA:** Days thirty to sixty?

**JAMES:** Run the AI-assisted process on that course. AI produces a first draft of the translated text, subtitles and, if appropriate, synthetic voice-over. A native-speaking vet reviews the clinical terminology. An editor checks the language and adapts examples where local practice differs, for instance drug names or regulations. Track time and cost at each step.

**NORA:** Sixty to a hundred?

**JAMES:** Launch the localised course to a small group of learners in that market, gather feedback on quality, and compare cost and time with the old process. If it works, build the playbook and pick the next five courses. At day one hundred, decide the roll-out plan and the investment needed. Then apply the same playbook to Finium's human healthcare content.

**NORA:** And who owns it?

**JAMES:** One person responsible for content operations, with authority over the production process, and a clinical lead who signs off quality. Clinical accuracy can't be delegated to a tool.

**NORA:** Let's do a second walk-through, from the production side. Invented.

**JAMES:** Meet Marco, a content producer at our hypothetical version of the company. Today, launching a postgraduate module in a new language might go like this. He sends the scripts to a translation agency. Weeks later, the translation comes back. A native-speaking vet reviews it and finds that some clinical terms were translated literally rather than using the terms vets actually use. Corrections go back and forth. Then the video needs subtitles, which means another vendor and another round of review. Months pass.

**NORA:** And with AI?

**JAMES:** Marco runs the scripts through an AI translation tool that's been given a glossary of approved clinical terms in that language, built with the reviewing vet. The tool produces the translation and subtitles in a day. The reviewing vet spends a few days checking and correcting, focusing on clinical meaning rather than basic language. Marco adapts a couple of examples where local practice differs. The module is ready in weeks, not months.

**NORA:** And the glossary improves each time.

**JAMES:** Exactly. Every correction goes into the glossary, so the next module is better. Over time, the company builds a valuable asset: a clinically validated multilingual terminology base. That's useful for veterinary and, potentially, human healthcare content.

**NORA:** What could go wrong?

**JAMES:** The obvious risk is quality. A mistranslated drug dose or procedure step could be dangerous, and would damage the brand badly. So clinical review must stay mandatory. The other risk is trying to translate everything at once. Start with a few high-demand courses and prove it.

### Lessons for other businesses

**NORA:** Widen out. Lessons for other businesses?

**JAMES:** Four. First, in expert-led businesses, use AI to protect expert time. Improve's value comes from specialists. AI should take the routine work off their plate, not try to replace them.

**NORA:** Second?

**JAMES:** Second, translation is one of the most underrated AI opportunities. Any business with content, documentation or training in more than one language should look hard at AI-assisted localisation. The quality has improved enormously, and with expert review, it can be both faster and cheaper.

**NORA:** Third?

**JAMES:** Third, when your customers consolidate, your sales model has to change. As vet practices merged into groups, training providers had to learn to sell to centralised buyers. The same is true in many industries, from dentistry to accounting.

**NORA:** And fourth?

**JAMES:** Fourth, a quiet company should think about what its public footprint says. Improve may be doing well, but from the outside, very little is visible. In a market where learners and employers research providers online, and increasingly through AI assistants, clear public information about leadership, programmes and results is part of selling.

**NORA:** A fifth?

**JAMES:** Yes. Adjacent markets are often defined by capability, not by customer. Improve's move into human healthcare looks odd if you think of it as a vet company. It makes more sense if you think of it as a professional education company that happens to have started with vets. Many businesses have a capability that would serve a different customer group, and AI can make it cheaper to adapt their product for that new group.

**NORA:** And for a small training provider listening?

**JAMES:** Try AI translation on one course and get an expert to check it. Try AI-drafted feedback on assignments, with you editing. You'll quickly find out where it saves time and where it doesn't.

### Risks and what to watch

**NORA:** Risks.

**JAMES:** One, AI disruption of the revenue model, as cheap self-paced content and general AI reduce what vets will pay for basic CPD. Two, low-cost webinar competitors in the same space. Three, dependence on UK vet practice spending, which is affected by staffing and by the economics of practice groups. Four, integration and key-person risk, after several ownership changes and an expansion into human healthcare.

**NORA:** And AI-specific risks?

**JAMES:** Clinical accuracy, first and foremost. Any AI-generated or AI-translated content must be checked by qualified people. Academic integrity is another. If learners use AI to write case reports, assessments have to adapt, for example by emphasising practical skills, oral discussion and real case data. And data protection, since learners' work and assessments are personal data, and case reports may include details about clients and their animals.

**NORA:** Anything about running an international business?

**JAMES:** The usual ones, in general. Different regulatory systems in each country, currency movements if revenue and costs are in different currencies, and the challenge of building a brand in markets where local providers are well established. And if the company relies on AI translation, it has to make sure local reviewers are genuinely expert, because a course that reads as machine-translated will damage trust quickly in a professional audience.

**NORA:** And the regulatory side?

**JAMES:** In general, providers of recognised qualifications have to satisfy accrediting bodies. If AI is used in marking, accreditors may want to understand how. Being open about that, and keeping humans responsible for final marks, is the safe path.

**NORA:** What should listeners watch?

**JAMES:** Three things. First, any public leadership and strategy announcements, which would give a clearer picture. Second, new language editions or international launches, which would signal the localisation opportunity being pursued. Third, any visible cooperation with Suveto, or any further acquisitions, in veterinary or human healthcare education.

**NORA:** And a warning sign?

**JAMES:** Price cutting in basic CPD without a clear move up the value chain. That would suggest the business is being squeezed rather than shaping its market.

### Quick-fire round

**NORA:** Quick-fire round. Short answers.

**JAMES:** Go.

**NORA:** What does Improve sell?

**JAMES:** Career-long learning for vets and their teams.

**NORA:** Most valuable asset?

**JAMES:** Its specialist-built course catalogue and its reputation in postgraduate vet education.

**NORA:** Biggest weakness?

**JAMES:** Reliance on scarce specialist time, and very little public visibility.

**NORA:** Best AI bet?

**JAMES:** AI-assisted course localisation and production.

**NORA:** Second best?

**JAMES:** AI-assisted marking and formative feedback.

**NORA:** Will AI replace vet tutors?

**JAMES:** No. It will help them mark faster and teach the parts only they can teach.

**NORA:** Most interesting strategic question?

**JAMES:** What Improve and Suveto could do together under the same owner.

**NORA:** Optimist or pessimist?

**JAMES:** Cautiously optimistic. Steady, regulated demand and a clear AI opportunity, but we're judging from very little public data.

### Wrap-up

**NORA:** Let me sum up. Improve International is a Swindon-based provider of postgraduate and continuing professional development training for vets and veterinary teams, delivered online, blended and in person. It has passed through several owners, including Benchmark Holdings and a management buyout backed by RJD Partners, and Levine Leichtman invested alongside management in July 2024. It has expanded into human healthcare education by acquiring Finium in Italy. Public information is very thin: no confirmed leaders, size or dates for most news, and no visible AI activity. The market has steady demand from CPD requirements, but faces consolidation of buyers, staff shortages and price pressure in basic CPD. Our view is that the best AI bet is localising and producing courses faster, with marking support close behind, always with specialists in charge of clinical quality.

**JAMES:** That's a fair summary. And my closing thought is that in professional education, AI's biggest gift isn't replacing the teacher. It's giving every learner faster feedback and giving every expert more time to do the part only an expert can do.
